title: Cheesy Carrot & Zucchini Orzo
servings: about 4 kid portions (batch cooks and freezes)
ingredients: 450 ml low-salt chicken or vegetable stock (scant 2 cups)
steps: Heat the oil or butter in a pan over medium-high. Add the garlic, grated carrot and grated zucchini and fry 2-3 min, until soft and fragrant.
Add the orzo and the stock. Stir and bring to a boil.
Turn down to medium and cook 10 min, stirring occasionally so it does not catch on the bottom.
When the orzo is soft, take it off the heat and stir through the grated cheddar. Serve.
notes: The recipe is from a UK baby/toddler account - courgette is zucchini, and it is written as a weaning recipe, suitable from 6 months. THE STOCK IS THE POINT: 450 ml to 190 g orzo is a tight ratio on purpose, so the orzo absorbs almost all of it and goes creamy like a risotto rather than being boiled and drained. Stir every couple of minutes - it will stick and scorch if you walk away. If it tightens up before the orzo is soft, splash in a little more stock or water. CHEESE OFF THE HEAT, always - cheddar stirred into a boiling pan goes stringy and oily. LOW-SALT STOCK matters if a baby or toddler is eating it; regular stock is far too salty for them. For adults it will taste underseasoned - salt and pepper your own bowl at the table rather than the pan. STORING (her numbers): fridge up to 4 days, freezer up to 3 months. It thickens hard as it cools, so loosen with a splash of water or stock when reheating. Grate the veg finely, not coarsely - fine grating is what makes it disappear into the sauce, which is the whole trick with kids.

title: Game Day Pretzel Bites
ingredients: Coarse salt (pretzel salt or coarse kosher)
steps: Heat the oven to 425F and line a sheet pan with parchment.
Cut each biscuit into 6 pieces - 48 bites total.
Bring the water to a boil in a wide pot, then add the baking soda SLOWLY - it foams up hard the second it hits boiling water.
Drop the biscuit pieces into the bath for 20-30 seconds, working in batches so they are not crowded. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and set them on the parchment.
Brush each bite with melted butter and sprinkle with coarse salt.
Bake 12-15 min, until deep golden brown.
notes: THE BAKING SODA BATH IS THE WHOLE TRICK - do not skip it. The alkaline water is what browns the outside and gives you actual pretzel flavor and chew; without it these are just baked biscuit pieces. Add the baking soda to the boiling water a spoonful at a time or it will foam over the pot. 20-30 seconds is enough; leave them longer and they get soapy and slick. WHAT A COMMENTER REPORTED: plain was about a 6/10, but tossed in garlic and parmesan before baking plus more melted butter after the bake it was a 12; a cinnamon sugar version was a 10. Worth doing half the batch savory and half sweet. Brushing again with butter right out of the oven is not in the original but it is what makes them taste like mall pretzels. SERVE: warm, with nacho/beer cheese sauce or grainy mustard. They go soft and tough within an hour or two, so time them to come out when people are ready to eat. 8-count biscuits cut in 6 gives 48 small bites; cut in 4 for bigger ones and add a minute or two in the oven.

title: Senate Bean Soup (Fast, Canned Beans)
source: NYT Cooking - Sarah DiGregorio (the recipe's own faster-version tip)
ingredients: 1 red or yellow onion, finely chopped
3 medium carrots, peeled and sliced 1/2 to 1 inch thick
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, Diamond Crystal (half the original Tbsp - see notes)
8 cups chicken broth (in place of the water)
4 (15-oz) cans navy beans, drained and rinsed
About 1 lb chopped ham (in place of the ham hocks)
1 medium russet potato, peeled and quartered
OPTIONAL: 8 oz kale, stems removed and chopped
steps: Melt the butter in a large soup pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring often, 5-6 min until softened.
Add the garlic and carrots and cook, stirring, about 2 min until the garlic is fragrant and softened.
Add the salt, smoked paprika, thyme and several generous grinds of black pepper. Stir to combine.
Add the broth, drained beans, chopped ham and potato. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a low simmer, cover, and simmer 20-30 min - until the potato is tender and the soup has come together.
Add the kale, if using, in the last 5 min.
Mash the potato pieces against the side of the pot with a fork. Stir vigorously to break down some of the beans too - that is what thickens it.
Stir in the cider vinegar. Taste and add salt and pepper as needed.
notes: This is the recipe's own TIP for a faster version, not a workaround: four 15-oz cans of navy beans for the dried, chopped ham for the ham hocks, chicken broth for the water, salt cut in half, and a 20-30 min simmer instead of the hour-plus. SALT: the original calls for 1 Tbsp kosher salt (Diamond Crystal) with plain water and unsalted dried beans; the tip says halve it, so 1 1/2 tsp. Even that can run high once you factor in salted broth, canned beans and ham - if you are using regular (not low-sodium) broth, start at 1 tsp and season at the end. If you use Morton kosher or table salt, cut it further; Diamond Crystal is much less salty by volume. RINSE THE BEANS - the canning liquid is starchy and salty. THICKENING: canned beans do not release starch the way a long simmer does, so the potato mash and crushing some of the beans matters more here than in the original. Still thin? Mash more beans or simmer a few minutes uncovered. The vinegar at the end is not optional - it is what keeps it from tasting flat. The full 1 hr 45 min version with dried navy beans and two smoked ham hocks is at the link.
